title: Adjudication reports may be withheld for security reasons, but redaction is preferred over silence
content:
A.1.5.9.3 says the Core Facilitator "should issue a report at the conclusion of their adjudication" on the Sky Forum, summarizing findings and reasoning — but only "where feasible." The Action Tenet at A.1.5.9.3.0.4.1 annotates that qualifier: it "means that the Core Facilitator has discretion to determine whether it is appropriate to issue a Public Report." Where a proceeding "involves sensitive security matters or evidence," the facilitator may "defer from issuing a public report entirely; or to issue a report that excludes the sensitive security matters, while maintaining as much transparency as possible. The latter option should be preferred where possible."

The interesting move is the explicit ranking of the two escape options. A discretion clause that simply permitted withholding would make silence and redaction equally available, and silence is always easier — nothing must be drafted, nothing can be challenged. Stating a preference converts the choice into one the facilitator must justify: publishing nothing is now the fallback from a fallback.

The security rationale is real given the surrounding regime. ACs are required to be anonymous (A.1.5.7), and adjudications frequently concern opsec breaches, so a detailed public report could complete the exposure the proceeding is about. Full transparency here would be self-defeating.

What is left unaddressed is the interaction with A.1.5.10.1, which requires that derecognition notices "are issued publicly, and justification and reasoning must be provided by the Core Facilitator" — with no feasibility qualifier. Read together, the outcome must always be public with reasons, while the adjudication report may be withheld. That is a coherent split, but it means the mandatory disclosure is the conclusion and the discretionary one is the analysis behind it.
description: A.1.5.9.3.0.4.1 reads 'where feasible' as facilitator discretion to skip a public report entirely, while directing that a report excluding sensitive matters is the preferred option.
